approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass Trail and Sahale Arm to Sahale Glacier Camp
approach_variants.hours: 4-5 to camp, about 2 more to the summit
approach_variants.notes: Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead, a large lot at road's end at 3,600 ft. This is the only approach on this list that is on maintained trail almost the whole way. The Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks up through old-growth timber — roughly 35 switchbacks, about 1,800 ft in the first two miles — then eases through meadows to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft, 3.5-3.7 miles in. At the pass take the left (north) fork for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open ridge crest, about another 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft, to Sahale Glacier Camp at roughly 7,200-7,600 ft — rock-walled tent pads on the moraine, and the NPS-permitted high camp. Water is reliable at the creek crossings low on the trail, at Doubtful Lake (a signed spur, about a mile and 1,000 ft down and back) and from snowmelt near Sahale Glacier Camp early and mid season. Sources dry up late summer, so fill before the long switchback climb. Above camp the Sahale Glacier is small and low-angle by North Cascades standards but should still be treated as a glacier — rope up rather than assuming it out. Overnight camping is quota-limited and needs a North Cascades backcountry permit picked up in person at Marblemount.
hazards: Loose rock on the summit block, with parties directly above and below on a popular route
Exposed class 3-4 scrambling — many parties belay the last section
Meltwater runnels on the glacier disguising real crevasses late season
Water sources dry by late summer between the trailhead and Doubtful Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing is the summit pyramid above the glacier, and the mistake to avoid is attacking it straight on.

From the top of the glacier you arrive under the southwest side of the summit block. Do not start up the steepest ground directly in front of you. Trend right toward the notch, then onto the north/east side of the block — the correct line corkscrews around the peak rather than going up it. You should find yourself on a system of solid but increasingly exposed class 3 ledges, not on a face.

The last confirmation is a short class 4 move — about twenty feet of it, one awkward crack or chimney-like exit that puts you through a notch in the summit rocks onto the top. There is a fixed rappel station at that spot, and finding a fixed anchor is the clearest proof from the ground that you are on the standard line and not a variation.

The trap is the dihedral. Left of the standard notch there is a steeper dihedral feature that reads as the obvious line; it goes at fourth to low fifth class on loose rock and wants gear. If you are looking at a clean-cut corner rather than a rubble ledge that leads around and right, you are on the harder variation.

In poor visibility: the block is small and unmistakable once you are at it, so the navigation problem is the glacier, not the rock. Late season the glacier surface is cut by meltwater runnels that look like crevasses and crevasses that look like runnels — parties report going up and climber's right, climbing diagonally across the gullies, because that side reads more reliably.

approach_variants.name: Car-to-car day push
approach_variants.notes:
Because the approach is on maintained trail to about 7,200 ft, Sahale is regularly done in a single long day from the trailhead, which sidesteps the quota-limited high camp entirely. The trade is that you carry glacier gear the whole 6 miles up and 6 miles down, and you meet the summit block later in the day when it is busiest and the snow is softest.

Nothing about the line changes; only the logistics do. If the permit lottery has closed you out of Sahale Glacier Camp, this is the fallback rather than a different route.
hazards: Long day with glacier gear carried the full distance
Arriving at the summit block in the afternoon queue
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical to the camp version — the pyramid above the top of the Sahale Glacier, gained by trending right to the notch and following ledges around the block to the short class 4 exit at the fixed rappel station.

itinerary.cal: Sahale Glacier Camp is one of the most sought-after permits in North Cascades NP; get an early-access wilderness permit or a walk-up the day before at the Marblemount ranger station.

days.note: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead, switchback up to Cascade Pass (3.7 mi, ~1,800 ft), then continue up the Sahale Arm climbers' trail to the permitted camp at ~7,600 ft. The final 0.6-0.7 mi above the Arm is loose scree/talus on cairns with real exposure — go slow and watch weather.
days.title: Approach to Sahale Glacier Camp

days.note: An early start to cross the small, crevassed Sahale Glacier while snow is firm, then a class 2-3 scramble to the 8,680 ft summit. Most parties return to camp, break it down, and hike all the way out to the car the same day rather than spend a second night.
days.title: Summit push and hike out

schedule.label: Rope up and gear up at camp
schedule.detail: Crampons/axe (and rope for glacier travel) go on before leaving camp.

schedule.label: Leave camp, cross the Sahale Glacier
schedule.detail: Firm morning snow makes crevasse crossing safer and faster.

schedule.label: Class 2-3 scramble to the summit block
schedule.detail: Loose rock near the top; some parties place a hand line.

schedule.label: Summit (8,680 ft)
schedule.detail: Views over Boston Basin and the Ptarmigan Traverse peaks.

schedule.label: Back at camp, break it down
schedule.detail: Pack up the tent and overnight gear for the descent.

schedule.label: Descend Sahale Arm and Cascade Pass trail
schedule.detail: 5.9 mi / 3,940 ft down; most parties reach the trailhead by late afternoon.

days.objective: Climb Sahale Mountain via the Sahale Glacier, then descend to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A popular 1-night backpack: ~13 mi round trip and ~5,000 ft gain, with an alpine-start glacier crossing and summit scramble on day 2 before hiking all the way out.

pitch_detail.notes: 3.7 mi, 1,700 ft gain on maintained trail
Continue north on the Sahale Arm climbers' trail; totals 5.9 mi / 3,940 ft gain from the trailhead to camp (7,600 ft)
pitch_detail.pitch: Cascade Pass to Sahale Glacier Camp

pitch_detail.notes: Rope up and ascend the Sahale Glacier to the southwest side of the summit pyramid; watch for crevasses, especially late season
Short chimney-like feature on the south side; a few pieces of rock pro protect the final moves; slung block on top serves as a rappel anchor
